div.p: Cloud computing has aroused great interest from both academia and industry in the past decade. Due to Service Level Agreement (SLA), the cloud service providers have to guarantee the reliability of their systems. However, unpredictable hardware or software failures are usually inevitable. For realtime tasks, system failure may cause them to miss their deadlines. Fault tolerance technique can efficiently avoid such cases. Primary-backup model is widely used to realize fault tolerance by duplicating a task into two copies -a primary copy and a backup copy. The redundancy introduced by backup copies incurs extra overhead for cloud systems. To address this issue, in this paper we propose a real-time fault-tolerant scheduling algorithm with rearrangement (RFTR) in cloud systems. Different from traditional scheduling algorithms, RFTR dynamically rearranges the execution orders of tasks. Simulation experiments are conducted on CloudSim platform. Compared with the existing scheduling algorithm FESTAL, RFTR shows excellent performance in both task schedulability and resource conservation.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Cloud computing provides users with convenient computing services. It has the characteristics of rapid elasticity, measured service and on-demand self-service [1]. Virtualization offers the possibility to dynamically expand or reduce the resources [2]. In cloud systems, the basic computing node is virtual machine (VM) instead of physical host. Large scale cloud systems accommodate tens of thousands of servers and consume large amounts of energy. It is a tough problem to adjust the resource allocation and optimize the resource utilization.

Nowadays with the rapid development of information technology and the growth of network bandwidth, more and more vendors provide real-time services for consumers, e.g., realtime communication, real-time surveillance and fast navigation. In real-time systems, the correctness of results depends not only on the logicality of the results but also on the time at which the results are produced [3]. Missing deadlines can cause degraded quality or unavailable service.

In addition to real-time requirements, fault tolerance is also a significant property of cloud computing. Fault tolerance provides guarantee of timeliness and safety for real-time systems in case of failure. Since hot backup brings considerable system overhead, seeking methods with high resource utilization has become a tendency of fault tolerance technology.

In this paper, we consider the dynamic scheduling issue for real-time tasks in cloud systems. We present an improved fault-tolerant scheduling algorithm with rearrangement RTFR based on the existing algorithm proposed by Wang et al. in [4]. RFTR is able to adaptively optimize the execution orders of real-time tasks and fully utilize the computing resources. Primary-backup (PB) approach is adopted to realize fault tolerance. After a primary copy completes, the corresponding backup copy will be deallocated so as to release the resource it occupies. Besides, the waiting tasks can be rearranged to utilize the released resource, whereas in most existing algorithms the executing sequence is settled after sending tasks to the waiting queue of a VM.

The remaining part of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews some related work about this topic. Section 3 gives the assumptions and notations about the fault tolerance model. Section 4 deals with the rearrangement mechanism. In Section 5, simulation results evaluate the performance of RFTR. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the major contribution of this work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Since scheduling tasks in multiprocessor system has been proved to be NP-hard [5], a large number of heuristic algorithms for assigning tasks have been developed. Bertossi et al. proposed Fault-Tolerant Rate-Monotonic First-Fit (FTRMFF) [6] by extending the RMFF algorithm and combining backup overbooking and deallocation [7]. Luo et al. proposed Tercos algorithm, which terminates the execution of active backup copies when corresponding primary copies successfully completed [8]. Unfortunately, these works only consider homogenous instead of heterogeneous systems which comprise different types of computing nodes with various processing capabilities. In addition, these algorithms are preemptive, which means an executing task can be preempted by another task. However, we prefer to consider non-preemptive tasks because context switch would introduce system overhead and time delay. Besides, some algorithms schedule tasks with precedence constraints [9]- [11], whereas we consider independent tasks. Because tasks with precedence constraints can also be scheduled by transforming the precedence graph into independent nodes with new ready times and deadlines [12].

However, none of the fault-tolerant scheduling algorithms mentioned above take virtualization into account. Recently, Wang et al. proposed a fault-tolerant method FESTAL, which extends the primary-backup model to schedule real-time tasks in clouds [4]. FESTAL considers both virtualization and backup overlapping, thereby providing high system utilization. Nonetheless, it lacks dynamic optimization of execution orders.

div.head: III. FAULT-TOLERANT SCHEDULING MODEL A. Fault-Tolerance Model
div.p: Some assumptions are made for the fault tolerance model: 1) When a host fails, all VMs on this host break down.

2) Faults are independent. That is to say, a faulty host can not cause incorrect behaviours in a non-faulty host. 3) There exists a failure detection mechanism. The failure of a host is detected as soon as failure happens. 4) A second failure does not occur before the system recovers from the former failure. This is in line with the actual situation where Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) is large enough.

div.head: B. Scheduling Model
div.p: A task t i is identified by a tuple (a i ,l i ,d i ), where a i is the arrival time, l i is the task length (in Million Instruction, or MI) and d i is the deadline. Each task t i has a primary copy t P i and a backup copy t always executes even in fault free case. Backupbackup (BB) overlapping is adopted, which means backup copies are allowed to overlap in time.
The scheduling criteria are analyzed in [4]. We briefly list the core principles here.

div.head: B. Rearrangement Mechanism
div.p: In traditional scheduling algorithms, once a task is sent to a VM, its start time is settled. This paper proposes the rearrangement mechanism which allows the waiting tasks to change their execution sequences. The rearrangement process is triggered by completion of primary copies. Suppose vm(t B n ) = vm jk , when primary copy t P n finishes executing, t B n is deallocated from vm jk and the waiting primary copies on vm jk are rearranged according to the procedure in Algorithm 1. All primary copies on vm jk are scanned and checked if they can utilize the time interval left by the deallocated backup copy (see lines 1-5). If any primary copy can advance its execution, its start time, finish time and the status of its corresponding backup copy are updated (see lines 6-10). The rearrangement mechanism optimizes the execution orders of waiting primary copies and brings significant improvement in increasing resource utilization.

div.head: C. Primary and Backup Scheduling
div.p: The rearrangement mechanism can be extended to integrate any dynamic scheduling algorithm. In this paper, RFTR is based on FESTAL. FESTAL is a fault-tolerant algorithm that extends from the conventional PB model by accommodating the virtualization technology and the VM migration technology which are employed in most cloud date centers. div.head: V. SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS
div.p: In this section, we present several groups of experiments to evaluate the performance of RFTR compared with FESTAL. We use two metrics to evaluate the performance of RFTR. The first is the guarantee ratio, which is defined as the number of tasks meeting their deadlines divided by the number of tasks arrived. The second metric is the number of VMs created during the experiment.

div.head: A. Simulation Method and Parameters
div.p: We choose CloudSim [13] as our simulation tool. CloudSim is a simulation platform that can be extended by users to test their methods, policies and mechanisms for managing cloud infrastructures. Similar to the settings in [4], each host is modeled to have processing capacity equivalent to 1000, 1500 or 2000 MIPS. There are three types of VM templates with processing capacities equivalent to 200, 300 and 400 MIPS. The time for turning on a host and creating a VM is 90 and 15 seconds respectively.

div.head: B. Simulation Results
div.p: Fig. 123show simulation results for the impact of task count, arrival rate and deadline on system performance respectively.

Fig. 1(a) shows that with the increase of the task count, the guarantee ratios of the RFTR and FESTAL are overall stable. This is because the cloud system is extensible. When more and more tasks arrive, new hosts are turned on and new VMs are created to ensure the guarantee ratio. Besides, RFTR and FESTAL have nearly the same guarantee ratios. Fig. From Fig. 2(a), we can see that with the decrease of task arrival rate, the guarantee ratios increase slowly. Because lower arrival rate means lower demand on system processing capacity. In addition, the system can provide enough hosts and VMs to accommodate the tasks under heavy load, so the fluctuation of guarantee ratios is not obvious. RFTR and FESTAL basically have almost the same guarantee ratios.

It can be observed from Fig. 2(b) that with the decrease of task arrival rate, the VM count decreases sharply. When the task arrival rate is high, the cloud system is not capable enough to meet the real-time requirements of such densely arrived tasks, so more VMs are created. When the task arrival rate becomes lower, a smaller number of VMs are able to deal with the new tasks. Compared with FESTAL, RFTR needs 10.8% less VMs on average. This can be attributed to the rearrangement mechanism adopted by RFTR, which utilize more idle time slots to accommodate more tasks.

Fig. 3(a) shows that looser deadlines bring higher guarantee ratios. When the deadlines are tight, the system is unable to deal with too many tasks. When the deadlines are loose enough, almost all tasks can meet the timing requirements and the guarantee ratios are nearly 100%.

In Fig. 3(b), the effect of rearrangement mechanism is evident. RFTR needs the 19.8% less VMs than FESTAL, which verifies the effectiveness of the rearrangement mechanism. The VM count increases with the increasing of baseDeadline because more tasks are accepted and thus more VMs are needed.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we consider the problem of scheduling realtime tasks in cloud systems. We propose a novel fault-tolerant scheduling algorithm that dynamically rearrange the execution orders of tasks. The RFTR algorithm considers the problem of increasing resource utilization and providing fault tolerance for real-time tasks in cloud systems. RFTR inherits the advantages of FESTAL and makes effective improvements in optimizing the resource utilization. The experiment results show that our approach outperforms FESTAL in terms of resource conservation while achieving almost the same guarantee ratios.
